body.en:
Heights are normally distributed with \(\mu=170\) cm and \(\sigma=10\) cm. Find the probability that a randomly chosen person has height between 160 and 185 cm.

\[P(160\leq X\leq185)=P(-1\leq Z\leq1.5)=\Phi(1.5)-\Phi(-1)=0.9332-0.1587=0.7745.\]

caption.en: Normal distribution model with mean \(\mu = 170\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = 10\), showing shaded area \(P(160 \le X \le 185) \approx 0.7745\) (\(-1 \le Z \le 1.5\)).

body.en:
• Permutations vs. Combinations: Use permutations \({}_nP_r = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\) when order or position matters (e.g. race finishes, assigned officer roles, passwords). Use combinations \({}_nC_r = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}\) when order is irrelevant (e.g. groups, hands of cards, committee selections).
  • Mutually Exclusive vs. Independent: Events \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen together: \(P(A \cap B) = 0\), giving \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\). Events are independent if one event's outcome has no effect on the other: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)\). Do not conflate the two concepts!
  • Empirical Rule Benchmarks: For any normal distribution: \(\approx 68.3\%\) falls within \(\mu \pm 1\sigma\), \(\approx 95.4\%\) falls within \(\mu \pm 2\sigma\), and \(\approx 99.7\%\) falls within \(\mu \pm 3\sigma\).
  • Z-Score Standardizing: Always compute \(z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\). A negative \(z\)-score signifies an observation below the mean; never omit the negative sign.

label.en: Worked Example C — Algebraic Structure & Vieta's Root Relations

body.en:
Solve the quadratic equation \( x^2 - 13x + 36 = 0 \) and verify the sum and product of its roots.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Factor into binomials: \( (x - 4)(x - 9) = 0 \implies x = 4 \text{ or } x = 9 \).
  2. Check Vieta's formulas: sum \( = 4 + 9 = \mathbf{13} \) and product \( = (4)(9) = \mathbf{36} \).

label.en: Worked Example D — Algebraic Structure & Vieta's Root Relations

body.en:
Solve the quadratic equation \( x^2 - 10x + 25 = 0 \) and verify the sum and product of its roots.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Factor into binomials: \( (x - 5)(x - 5) = 0 \implies x = 5 \text{ or } x = 5 \).
  2. Check Vieta's formulas: sum \( = 5 + 5 = \mathbf{10} \) and product \( = (5)(5) = \mathbf{25} \).

question.en: In a class of 200 students taking a test with mean 65 and SD 12 (normally distributed), how many students would you expect to score above 80?

A committee of 4 members is to be selected at random from a club of 7 seniors and 5 juniors. (a) What is the total number of possible committees? (b) Find the probability that the committee contains exactly 2 seniors and 2 juniors.

solution.en:
(a) Order does not matter, so the total number of ways to choose 4 members from 12 total people is: \[\text{Total} = \binom{12}{4} = \frac{12 \times 11 \times 10 \times 9}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 495.\]

(b) Number of ways to choose 2 seniors from 7: \[\binom{7}{2} = \frac{7 \times 6}{2 \times 1} = 21.\]

Number of ways to choose 2 juniors from 5: \[\binom{5}{2} = \frac{5 \times 4}{2 \times 1} = 10.\]

By the fundamental counting principle, favorable outcomes: \[21 \times 10 = 210.\]

Probability: \[P(\text{2 seniors, 2 juniors}) = \frac{210}{495} = \frac{14}{33} \approx 0.4242 \quad (42.4\%).\]

question.en: [Probability & Statistics · Practice 3] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 5t + 5 \), evaluate \( g(8) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 50 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 8 \): \( g(8) = 5(8) + 5 = \mathbf{45} \). Setting \( 5t + 5 = 50 \) gives \( 5t = 45 \implies t = \mathbf{9} \).

question.en: [Probability & Statistics · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
